title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for an artificial intelligence education policy for university teaching and learning in the context of rapidly emerging text-generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The author argues that higher education institutions need clearer guidance on academic integrity, ethical use, privacy, accountability, access, and the pedagogical implications of AI adoption.

The study used a mixed-methods survey design with online questionnaires administered to 457 students and 180 teachers and staff members across Hong Kong universities. Quantitative items measured prior use of generative AI, perceptions of its educational value, concerns about misuse, and views on issues such as time-saving, personalized feedback, and the role of teachers. Open-ended responses were analyzed thematically to identify policy priorities and stakeholder concerns.

Findings suggest that respondents were cautiously optimistic about the educational potential of generative AI, especially for saving time, offering immediate feedback, improving digital competence, and supporting learning. At the same time, they expressed concerns about cheating, over-reliance, unequal access, weak ability to detect AI misuse, and risks to transferable skills. The paper concludes by proposing an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions, emphasizing training, ethical guidelines, monitoring, and a balanced human-centered approach to AI integration in higher education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed descriptive survey with qualitative thematic analysis, not an experimental or quasi-experimental comparison of AI coaching versus human feedback. It provides useful stakeholder evidence but does not meet higher causal inference criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceptions and policy implications only; it does not estimate observed learning gains or productivity effects. Reported positives are moderate and expectancy-based, so overall impact is unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: Text generative AI such as ChatGPT used as a university teaching-and-learning support tool, including personalized feedback, guidance for coursework, and AI-assisted support for student learning and teacher planning policy considerations.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a policy and stakeholder-perception study rather than an intervention efficacy trial. Across 457 students and 180 teachers/staff, respondents endorsed institutional planning for generative AI (students mean=4.5, teachers mean=4.54) and saw value in structured governance, training, and ethical guidelines for university teaching and learning.
finding.measure: Survey ratings on AI policy need, governance, training, and institutional planning; open-ended thematic responses

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived generative AI as useful for saving time and providing immediate, personalized support, but this was based on self-reported expectations rather than a controlled efficiency experiment. Students rated time savings highly (mean=4.23) and both groups endorsed personalized feedback (students mean=3.75; teachers mean=3.86).
finding.measure: Survey ratings on time saving and personalized/immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: Respondents believed generative AI could support digital competence and some academic skills, but also worried about over-reliance, reduced critical thinking, and weaker transferable skills. For example, teachers reported concern about over-reliance (mean=4.24), while respondents also endorsed possible gains in digital competence (students mean=3.8; teachers mean=3.83).
finding.measure: Survey ratings and thematic comments on digital competence, critical thinking, teamwork, and transferable skills
